title: test(driver-sql): attribute each legacyUniqueReplacements guard to exactly one case (#8557)
body:
Fixes #8557

Per-guard **attribution** for `legacyUniqueReplacements` in
`packages/drivers/driver-sql/src/schema-drift.ts` (the function is at `:1101`,
the declared-index arm at `:1165`, on this branch's merge base). One new test
file, no source change, no behaviour change.

⛔ **The existing object-level tests are untouched.** Section 5 of
`sql-driver-declared-index-organization-respelling.test.ts` and the
`*-organization-unique` suites stay exactly as they are — they are deliberately
*broader* than any single guard, which is precisely why they could not do this
job. This PR adds attribution; it substitutes nothing.

## The premise, re-measured on today's tree

The card's six ablations were measured on an older tree, so both negatives were
re-run at this branch's merge base. **Both are still individually unpinned** —
the card is still live and does not shrink:

| card ablation | measured then | measured now |
|---|---|---|
| **C1** — remove the explicitly-named-index guard | RED | **RED** |
| **C2** — remove `legacyName === replacement.name` (ADR-0120 S6) | GREEN | **GREEN** |
| **C3** — admit a declared bare `unique: true` through the filter | GREEN | **GREEN** |

## What landed

`schema-drift.legacy-unique-guard-attribution.test.ts` — 15 cases over the
arm's **14** early-exits, inventoried in the file header so completeness stays
checkable when a guard is added.

**Section A — 9 individually attributable guards.** One input per guard,
constructed so only that guard can reject it. Every case carries a **twin**:
the same input with the single property that guard reads changed, which must
produce exactly one replacement. The twin is the reachability witness — without
it, a case asserting `[]` would keep passing while some *earlier* guard swallowed
the input, which is the same "green pin narrower than its name" failure this
card is about, one level up.

**Section B — 5 guards that cannot be attributed at all.** Not because the test
is hard to write: another guard rejects a strict superset of their inputs, so
deleting one is behaviour-preserving for *every possible argument* and any test
claiming to pin it would be lying. For those, what is pinned is **the fact the
domination rests on**, so the day it breaks and the guard becomes load-bearing
alone, something goes red. This is the answer to C2 and C3: the S6 composite is
double-guarded and the bare spelling triple-guarded, so their guards are
unpinnable by construction, and the reachable failures are pinned instead.

The S6 objects are pinned directly, in both the shipped bare-`true` spelling and
the respelled `'organization'` form — `sys_team`, `sys_business_unit` and
`sys_member`, transcribed from the object definitions and verified against them
(`{ fields: ['name', 'organization_id'], unique: true }`,
`{ fields: ['code', 'organization_id'], unique: true }`,
`{ fields: ['organization_id', 'user_id'], unique: true }`; the organization
column lands last in two and first in the third, so both key orders are
exercised).

## The C3 half of an already-shipped pair

#8463 (PR #8512, `4fccace74`) landed in this same file three hours before the
card was filed, putting the declared-vs-field bare-`true` divergence into
**prose** on `isOrganizationScopedUnique`'s JSDoc (`schema-drift.ts:83-102` on
this branch's merge base). Verified on today's tree: that prose had no
attributing test, and ablation C3 measures exactly that gap from the test side.
The bare-spelling case here is the **missing test-side half of that one
decision**, not a coincidental second finding. Routing the declared branch
through the field predicate stays the rejected option 1 of #8323 (maintainer
ruling 2026-08-13) and is now refused by a test rather than only by a comment.

## Verification — the ablation matrix IS the acceptance test

Each guard deleted, suites re-run, guard restored, direction predicted before
running. 18 ablations across both the new file and the object-level suite
(41 tests). **All 18 matched prediction**, with one divergence noted below.

Every one of the 9 section-A guards turns **exactly one** new test red, and its
name says which line went:

| guard removed | new tests red |
|---|---|
| `!physicalColumns.has(tenantField)` | 1 — unmaterialized tenant column |
| `!isOrganizationScopedUnique(field.unique)` | 1 — explicit `global` field |
| `name === tenantField` | 1 — unique on the tenant column |
| `!physicalColumns.has(name)` | 1 — field has no column |
| `legacyNames.length === 0` | 1 — both legacy spellings declared |
| `idx?.unique !== 'organization'` | 1 — non-unique declared index |
| explicitly-named-index guard (**C1**) | 1 (+1 pre-existing object-level) |
| `!listed.every(physicalColumns.has)` | 1 — unmaterialized declared column |
| `declaredNames.has(legacyName)` | 1 (+1 pre-existing object-level) |

The 5 dominated guards behave as section B claims — `!tenantField`,
`!isUniqueScopeDeclared`, `listed.length === 0`, `!replacement` and
`legacyName === replacement.name` (**C2**) each leave all 41 tests green when
deleted alone, and **C3** leaves all 41 green — which is why they are pinned as
dominations. Their joint ablations do go red, confirming the domination is what
holds them:

- `listed.length === 0` **+** `!replacement` together: red on the section-B
  joint pin (the null dereference the two mutually prevent).
- S6 guard **+** `declaredNames` (card **D1**): 4 red, including the S6
  composites case and the object-level S6 test.
- bare-spelling admitted **+** S6 **+** `declaredNames` (card **D3**): 7 red,
  including the bare-spelling case in both suites.

**One divergence from prediction, reported as measured.** The D3 combination
also reddens the `legacyNames.length === 0` field-arm case, which I had not
predicted. Cause: that fixture must declare indexes at all (that is how
`declaredNames` gets populated), and under D3 the *declared* arm starts claiming
the same fixture. Its single-guard isolation is unaffected — the case is
documented in place rather than respelled, because spelling it immune to
multi-guard ablation would cost the realistic #3955 shape.

`!tenantField` is the one guard whose deletion is caught by **tsc**, not by any
test: it is the narrowing that makes `physicalColumns.has(tenantField)`
type-check. Measured — deleting it fails `pnpm --filter @objectstack/driver-sql
typecheck` with TS2322 while all 41 tests stay green. Stated in the test so a
future reader does not read "no test covers it" as "nothing covers it".

## Gates

Run at final HEAD `0e57ab953`, after the last commit:

`check:nul-bytes`, `check:test-source-alias`, `check:type-source-resolution`,
`check:query-options-erasure`, `check:type-check-coverage`,
`check:changeset-gate-self-tests`, `check:objectui-changeset`,
`check-adr-0087-registration`, `check-changeset-no-major`,
`check-empty-changeset` — all green; plus
`pnpm --filter @objectstack/driver-sql typecheck` and the package's full suite
(**97 files, 1663 passed, 55 skipped**).

The five changeset-family gates were **not** in the dispatched list — they were
surfaced by re-deriving `scripts/pm/dispatch-gates.mjs` against the settled diff
once the changeset existed.

`check:type-check-debt` is **not measured locally**: it refuses without a built
workspace closure (49 dependency packages lack a built type entry point here),
and its own error text is explicit that a number measured from an unbuilt tree
is a different world. Left to CI. It cannot move on this diff — `driver-sql`
carries no DEBT ledger entry, and its own `tsc --noEmit` is green with the new
file included.

Changeset: `patch` on `@objectstack/driver-sql`, with the bump level justified
in the file — no runtime change, but the pin is release-relevant and `none`
would leave it undocumented at the one moment anyone reads for it.
